sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Many modern language models have adopted hybrid architectures that incorporate both linear-time recurrence and softmax attention. Modern recurrence layers provide a highly expressive mixing mechanism while ensuring high throughput by compressing contextual information into a fixed-size state, but underperform softmax attention in contextual information retrieval. In this paper, we reveal a Competing Learning phenomenon where different kinds of mixers compete to learn the same function, and when any layer learns a function, it suppresses the corresponding learning signal for other layers. Layer attribution analysis reveals that under typical data distributions, modern recurrence learns retrieval functions faster than softmax attention, causing attention to fail to learn retrieval in most cases. Stopping weight updates in recurrence in the middle of training helps attention learn retrieval. Based on these results, we propose a staged training procedure for pre-training hybrid architectures on natural language. Empirical results on models up to 1B parameters show that our method results in substantial improvement in language modeling loss, common-sense reasoning, as well as a wide range of retrieval-related tasks across different context lengths.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Many modern language models have adopted hybrid architectures that incorporate both linear-time recurrence and softmax attention. Modern recurrence layers provide highly expressive mixing mechanism while ensuring high throughput by compressing contextual information into fixed-size state, but underperform softmax attention in contextual information retrieval. In this paper, we reveal Competing Learning phenomenon where different kinds of mixers compete to learn the same function, and when any layer learns function, it suppresses the corresponding learning signal for other layers. Layer attribution analysis reveals that under typical data distributions, modern recurrence learns retrieval functions faster than softmax attention, causing attention to fail to learn retrieval in most cases. Stopping weight updates in recurrence in the middle of training helps attention learn retrieval. Based on these results, we propose staged training procedure for pretraining hybrid architectures on natural language. Empirical results on models up to 1B parameters show that our method results in substantial improvement in language modeling loss, common-sense reasoning, as well as wide range of retrieval-related tasks across different context lengths.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recently, many open-weight large language models (LLMs) have adopted hybrid architectures that combine two distinct types of token mixers: linear recurrence (e.g., state space models (SSMs) and linear attention) and softmax attention (Vaswani et al., 2017). Such models have demonstrated strong language modeling capabilities while offering improved training and inference efficiency, scaling to models with up to trillions of parameters. Representative examples include Kimi K3 (Team Kimi et al., 2026), GLM-5.3-Flash (GLM Team, 2026), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Qwen Team, 2026), and Nemotron-3-Ultra (NVIDIA Team, 2026). Prior work has shown that, in well-trained LLMs, different token mixersand/or different heads within the same mixercan specialize in distinct mixing patterns. For instance, Xiao et al. (2025) show that subset of attention heads in Transformer models (Vaswani et al., 2017), referred to as retrieval heads, learn long-distance mixing patterns, whereas other heads primarily capture shortdistance interactions. Similarly, Bick et al. (2025) show that different heads within linear recurrence layer exhibit retrieval behaviors over different distances. In hybrid architectures, Chen et al. (2026) further show that assigning long-distance retrieval to softmax attention and short-distance mixing to recurrent layers is beneficial across wide range of downstream tasks. Together, these findings motivate division of labor in hybrid models, where softmax attention specializes in longdistance mixing while recurrent layers specialize in short-distance mixing. In this work, we identify Competing Learning, phenomenon in which layers that acquire retrieval capabilities earlier inhibit the development of these capabilities in other layers. In the hybrid models we study, recurrent layers tend to gain this early advantage, taking over retrieval-related functions that softmax attention layers are intended to specialize in. Consequently, training hybrid models using standard practices results in softmax attentions retrieval learning being limited by recurrent layers, leading to suboptimal division of labor. 1The code is released at https://github.com/thunlp/competing-learning. *Equal contributions.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Concretely, we provide an analysis based on layer-wise contribution attribution on synthetic retrieval tasks to identify the speed of retrieval learning of different mixers in hybrid model. The analysis provides evidence to illustrate how the learning of retrieval functions in softmax attention is inhibited by the retrieval learning of recurrent layers. Furthermore, manually stopping recurrent layers from learning retrieval at different points in the training process reveals that softmax attention starts learning retrieval as soon as recurrent layers learning is stopped. We also discover that under typical training distributions, with more short-distance patterns than long-distance ones, recurrence learns retrieval faster than softmax attention, resulting in suboptimal division of labor. To address this issue, we propose Better Layer Division (BLD), training pipeline that introduces preliminary training stage before standard pretraining to give full-attention layers an early advantage in learning retrieval. This intervention is designed to steer Competing Learning in favor of full-attention layers, encouraging them to assume the long-range retrieval role during subsequent pretraining. We evaluate BLD on widely used benchmarks (e.g. Common-sense reasoning (CSR), recall-intensive tasks, LongPPL (Fang et al., 2025).) using hybrid models based on Kimi Delta Attention (KDA)2 (Kimi Team et al., 2025) at multiple scales, and observe improvements in benchmarks including CSR, recall-intensive tasks, RULER, LongPPL and training loss over vanilla ones. Our main contributions are as follows: We investigate the training dynamics of layer-wise functional specialization in hybrid models, focusing on the allocation of retrieval-related functions between recurrent and fullattention layers. We identify and characterize Competing Learning through empirical analyses, revealing how early differences in retrieval learning influence subsequent layer specialization. We propose BLD, an LLM training pipeline that guides functional specialization by freezing the parameters of selected components during the early stage of pretraining, and verify its effectiveness on hybrid models at multiple scales and with different recurrent architectures. Empirical results show that BLD produces pretrained LLMs with performance gains on wide range of tasks.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Hybrid Architectures Recent LLMs increasingly adopt hybrid architectures that combine softmax attention with linear attention, including GLM-5.3-Flash (GLM Team, 2026), Kimi K3 (Team Kimi et al., 2026), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Qwen Team, 2026), and Nemotron-3-Ultra (NVIDIA Team, 2026). Such designs combine the retrieval strength of softmax attention with the computational efficiency of linear attention. Prior work has shown that linear or recurrent models can underperform softmax attention on precise in-context retrieval (Arora et al., 2024; Bick et al., 2025; Jelassi et al., 2024). Several works improve the memory or retrieval capabilities of linear attention through architectural or state-space enhancements (Yang et al., 2023; 2025b; Qin et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2026). In contrast, our work does not enhance the retrieval capacity of linear attention itself, but improves the pre-training of hybrid models without architectural modifications. Hybrid architectures instead retain softmax-attention layers for long-range retrieval while using efficient linear attention for most computation (Kimi Team et al., 2025). Our work focuses on better realizing this architectural complementarity during pre-training. Most of our experiments are conducted on Kimi-Linear-style models based on Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) (Kimi Team et al., 2025). Labor Division in Non-Hybrid Models Prior work has shown that only small subset of attention heads develops strong long-context retrieval behavior (Wu et al., 2025). DuoAttention exploits this functional specialization by distinguishing retrieval heads from streaming heads for efficient inference (Xiao et al., 2025). Other works leverage already-formed retrieval heads to construct posttraining signals for improving long-context performance and contextual faithfulness (Huang et al., 2025; Ma & Okazaki, 2026). Recent studies further analyze how retrieval heads are learned or evolve during context extension and long-context continual pre-training (Zhao et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2026). These works mainly study or exploit specialization among homogeneous softmax-attention heads, rather than the allocation of retrieval capability across heterogeneous attention components. 2Widely-used RNN architecture adopted by frontier models (e.g. Kimi K3, GLM-5.3-Flash).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: In hybrid models, however, such allocation is critical: if all retrieval heads emerge in linear-attention components, the intended architectural advantage of combining efficient linear attention with the stronger retrieval capability of softmax attention would be largely undermined. Labor Division in Hybrid Models Prior work has observed functional specialization between attention and recurrent components in hybrid models, with attention playing particularly important role in exact retrieval and recall (Bick et al., 2025; Afendulev et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025). These works mainly characterize specialization after it has emerged, while other studies exploit such specialization to construct hybrid models from pretrained Transformers (Chen et al., 2026; Bick et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). In contrast, we study how this division of labor forms during hybridmodel pre-training and how it can be actively optimized. In the work most closely related to ours, Qiao et al. (2026) show that efficient-attention modules can weaken the optimization pressure for full-attention layers and delay retrieval-head formation. Our work further identifies the underlying competition in retrieval-specific learning signals: linear-attention and softmax-attention layers both gradually acquire retrieval capabilities, and layers that learn retrieval earlier reduce the retrievalspecific prediction error, thereby weakening the learning signal available to other layers. We refer to this as the Competing Learning phenomenon and use it to guide pre-training toward stronger retrieval specialization in softmax-attention layers.

sections.title: 3 COMPETING LEARNING IN HYBRID ATTENTION MODELS
sections.content: Central to our paper is the Competing Learning phenomenon, which is stated as follows: Competing Learning Phenomenon During hybrid-model pre-training, both recurrent and softmax-attention layers can acquire in-context retrieval capabilities. If some layers learn retrieval earlier, they can reduce the retrieval-specific prediction error, weakning the training signal for other layers, slowing their acquisition of the same capability. To show the causes and effects of this phenomenon, we conduct series of layer attribution and gradient intervention experiments to monitor the retrieval learning of each layer in hybrid model. In the following sections, we first propose synthetic retrieval task (Section 3.1). Then, we propose novel metric for determining how much layer contributes to the models retrieval abilities (Section 3.2). Finally, we train series of hybrid models on this task and inspect the contributions of each layer to monitor their retrieval learning over time (Section 3.3). Concretely, we conduct the following three sets of experiments: Section 3.3.1: We provide the experimental evidence for the Competing Learning phenomenon with weight freezing. Section 3.3.2: We provide direct gradient evidence for the Competing Learning phenomenon through weight freezing and unfreezing. Section 3.3.3: We show how the distribution of short and long-distance patterns chooses the winner of Competing Learning phenomenon. Altogether, we demonstrate the existence of Competing Learning in hybrid models and that KDA layers learn modeling short-distance patterns faster than attention layers. Since short-distance patterns are more frequent than long-distance patterns in natural language pretraining (Futrell et al., 2015), this leads to suboptimal labor division in direct pretraining of hybrid models.

sections.title: 3.3 ANALYSIS EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: With the above task and estimation method, we can now perform series of experiments to analyze the phenomenon of Competing Learning for hybrid models, which is central to our paper. Experimental Configuration We train several hybrid models on the Spaced Retrieval task. Each model has 3.6M parameters and consists of two KDA (a widely-used linear recurrence architecture) layers and two attention layers. Unless specified otherwise, we use 1:1 mixtures of examples with = 64 and = 8192. During training, we only compute the loss on output tokens using loss masks. Here, we report the results for = 8192, but we emphasize that the results of = 64 are similar. The results for = 64 and more experimental details can be found in Appendix A.

sections.title: ANOTHER
sections.content: Without intervention, KDA layers become dominant in terms of retrieval ability in this setting, as shown in Figure 2. To investigate how their dominance affects the attention layers, we freeze all KDA layers at different training steps and continue training the remaining model components. As shown in the left part of Figure 4, the attention layers retrieval ability increases sharply immediately after each freezing intervention. This observation is consistent with the hypothesis that, once KDA layers acquire some retrieval capability, they suppress the acquisition of the same capability by attention layers, providing evidence for the Competing Learning phenomenon. Furthermore, we explore how unfreezing KDA layers at later training step influences learning competition. In the right plot of Figure 4, runs in which KDA is frozen earlier than step 125 have higher retrieval ability than when the KDA remains frozen for the rest of the training, while runs in which KDA is frozen later than step 125 have lower retrieval ability than when the KDA remains frozen. Moreover, these changes appear almost immediately after KDA is unfrozen. This clear polarization may be attributed to the fact that attention layers in checkpoints where freezing began

At these early freezing checkpoints, attention layers have already accumulated sufficient advantage in retrieval performance, substantially outperforming KDA layers. Consequently, once freezing is lifted, attention layers tend to further reinforce their retrieval capabilities, while KDA layers are driven to specialize in other functions. This is reflected in Figure 4: at checkpoints where attention layers have established sufficiently strong advantage, their retrieval ability further improves after unfreezing. In contrast, at checkpoints where this advantage is insufficient, attention layers are once again outcompeted by KDA layers, leading to decline in their retrieval ability. Takeaways In hybrid models, KDA and attention layers compete to learn retrieval, with KDA initially gaining an advantage due to its stronger inductive bias toward short-range patterns. Temporarily freezing the dominant KDA layers can shiftand, with sufficient duration, even reversethe winner of this competition.

Notably, the gradient norm increases progressively rather than abruptly, suggesting that this amplification emerges from the evolving optimization dynamics rather than as an immediate consequence of freezing. This supports Competing Learning: learning signals depend on the current ability gap of components, reinforcing the advantages of already dominant components.

sections.title: 3.3.3 DIFFERENT TRAINING DATA PREFER DIFFERENT ARCHITECTURES
sections.content: We further investigate how the distribution of gap (g) in the training data influences the learnability of retrieval in different mixers. To this end, we train the hybrid model using different mixture proportions of short-distance (g = 64) and long-distance (g = 8192) examples. As shown in Figure 3, attention layers become more important as the proportion of long-distance examples increases, whereas KDA layers are more likely to dominate when the long-distance patterns do not appear overwhelmingly more than short-distance patterns. This is because KDA initializes forget gates with low values, which gives this architecture short-distance inductive bias (See Appendix for more specific explanation). Takeaways Different mixers learn retrieval at different speeds, depending on the data distribution. While both mixers can acquire the same retrieval abilities, the mixer that learns faster will become dominant, limiting the learning of the other mixer. Implications Applying the traditional training recipe to hybrid model can lead to suboptimal division of labor. Because short-distance patterns occur more frequently than long-distance patterns in natural language (Futrell et al., 2015), the training objective may encourage KDA to dominate retrieval, suppressing the training of attention layers. This issue is less problematic in homogeneous architectures such as Transformers, where all layers share the same architecture and, consequently, have the same potential for retrieval.

sections.title: 4 LLM PRETRAINING EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: In this section, we show that we can leverage insights about Competing Learning to achieve improved LLM performance in natural language pre-training.

sections.title: 4.1 METHOD: BETTER LAYER DIVISION
sections.content: Based on the analysis results in Section 3.3.1, we propose Better Layer Division (BLD), which freezes RNN layers weights during the early stage of pretraining, thereby giving the attention lay-

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: ers first-mover advantage in Competing Learning. Importantly, this intervention establishes corrected division of labor between the two components, which is subsequently preserved and further reinforced throughout the remainder of pretraining. This better labor division translates to improved model performance.

sections.title: 4.2 EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS
sections.content: Model Configuration We train family of KDAattention hybrid models ranging from 180M to 1B total parameters, including embeddings. All models share repeating four-layer pattern consisting of one attention layer followed by three KDA layers, maintaining fixed 3:1 KDA-to-attention ratio across scales. The layers are stacked in the form of Attention-KDA-KDA-KDA, and all layers are using NoPE (not adopting RoPE, which is reported to be better than using RoPE in KDA-based hybrid architecture (Kimi Team et al., 2025)). We scale the models by varying their depth and hidden width. At each scale, BLD and vanilla pre-training use identical architectures. Detailed model configurations are provided in Appendix C. Training Configuration We compare BLD against vanilla pre-training by training models from scratch with token budgets scaled proportionally to their non-embedding parameter counts, following the Chinchilla scaling principle (training tokens are roughly 20 of parameters) (Hoffmann et al., 2022). All models are trained on DCLM (Li et al., 2024), high-quality open-source pretraining corpus, using the Qwen3 tokenizer (Yang et al., 2025a) and context length of 16,384 tokens. For BLD, the KDA blocks remain frozen for approximately 1/10 of the subsequently unfrozen pretraining part. The vanilla baseline updates all parameters, using the same training data, token budgets, and optimization schedule. We use AdamW during the initial portion of pre-training, followed by Muon with auxiliary AdamW after unfreezing, with identical optimization schedules for BLD and the vanilla baseline. Detailed hyperparameters and token budgets are provided in Appendix D. Evaluation Tasks We evaluate models across common-sense reasoning (CSR), recall-intensive tasks, RULER, and language modeling, without fine-tuning. See Appendix for more details. CSR is measured by the average score on seven benchmarks: ARC-Easy, ARCChallenge (Clark et al., 2018), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2019), LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016). Recall is evaluated on six tasks from the Based (Arora et al., 2024) evaluation suite: SWDE (Lockard et al., 2019), FDA (Arora et al., 2023), SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2018), TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), DROP (Dua et al., 2019), and Natural Questions (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019). RULER (Hsieh et al., 2024) is evaluated with average scores across the 57 evaluated RULER tasklength combinations spanning 1K to 16K tokens. Language modeling is evaluated using word-level perplexity on WikiText-2 (Merity et al., 2016) and selected-token perplexity on LongPPL (Fang et al., 2025).

sections.content: Downstream Tasks As shown in Table 1, BLD models achieve notably lower LM losses. They also show modest improvement in CSR performance, while exhibiting substantial gains on retrieval-oriented tasks, including Recall and RULER. Moreover, the PPL metrics, which reflect overall long-context modeling capability, consistently favor BLD by large margin. The specific subtask scores are included in Appendix F. Specifically, we calculated next-token prediction loss on Books3,BookCorpus2 (Gao et al., 2020) as function of token positions, up to 16K. sections.title: 4.4 TRANSFERABILITY TO OTHER RNN ARCHITECTURES
sections.content: We also applied BLD to two other popular recurrent mixers, Gated DeltaNet (GDN) (Yang et al., 2025b) and Gated Linear Attention (GLA) (Yang et al., 2023). These models have the same configuration as the model in Section 4.2, but with KDA layers replaced with either of these layers. Training configuration is also the same as in Section 4.2. Further details are reported in Appendix H. Takeaways The advantages of BLD, lower training loss and better downstream task performance, are transferable to other linear recurrence architectures.

sections.title: 4.5 EVIDENCE FOR LABOR DIVISION CHANGE IN ATTENTION SCORES
sections.content: We further provide direct evidence that BLD induces stronger functional differentiation. Specifically, following Xiao et al. (2025), we analyze 510M KDA-attention hybrid models by training α values to distinguish retrieval heads, which are responsible for long-distance information retrieval, from streaming heads, which primarily perform short-distance token mixing. α measures heads reliance on full-context attention, with larger values indicating greater reliance. In other words, heads with greater α values are more important for long-distance retrieval. The α values are trained for 1,000 steps. More experimental details and results are reported in Appendix I. As shown in Figure 9, the attention heads in the BLD model exhibit higher α values than those in the vanilla model, indicating that BLD contains more retrieval heads that attend to long-range tokens. Figure 7 reports models retrieval accuracy as attention heads are progressively masked in ascending order of their α values. For BLD, the accuracy remains largely unchanged as lowα heads are masked and drops sharply only when the final three heads, which have the highest α values, are removed. This suggests that these three heads play critical role in retrieval, and we therefore identify them as retrieval heads. In contrast, the vanilla model exhibits substantial accuracy drop only when its single highest-α head is masked, indicating that it contains only one retrieval head. Takeaways BLD promotes greater degree of functional specialization, with more attention heads specializing in long-range retrieval. This behavior aligns with the motivation underlying our method.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we first identify the Competing Learning phenomenon and provide supporting experimental evidence. We then show that directly pretraining hybrid models can lead to suboptimal division of labor among different architectural components. To address this issue, we propose BLD and validate its effectiveness through scalable experiments. By promoting more effective division of labor, BLD consistently improves model capabilities across wide range of dimensions. Nevertheless, BLD represents only preliminary approach to addressing the Competing Learning phenomenon in the training of hybrid models. We believe that deeper understanding of the Competing Learning phenomenon will provide further insights into the division of labor within hybrid architectures and inspire the development of more advanced neural architectures and training strategies that better account for this phenomenon and achieve stronger performance.

Each run continues from the saved training state, preserving the optimizer, learning-rate schedule, random state, and data order. Unfreezing does not reset these states or restart warmup. SHORT-DISTANCE INDUCTIVE BIAS FROM KDA FORGET GATES The KDA mechanism can be formulated as follows: St = (I βtktkT ) Diag(αt)St1 + βtktvT Rdkdv , ot = ST qt Rdv . (8) Here, αt denotes the forget gate, which is initialized with relatively small values. Consequently, the KDA state St initially tends to retain information primarily from recent tokens. This is because historical information is progressively attenuated by the forget gates, and the cumulative product of small gate values rapidly approaches zero over successive time steps. As result, contributions from distant tokens diminish quickly.

sections.title: E EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: E.1 CHECKPOINT AND METRIC SELECTION We evaluate the final pretraining checkpoint without fine-tuning, using zero demonstrations for the downstream language-model evaluation tasks. The decoding strategy for generation tasks is greedy decoding. Language Modeling Loss We report the mean training loss over the final 100 optimizer updates. Common-Sense Reasoning CSR is the macro average of seven tasks: ARC-Easy and ARCChallenge (Clark et al., 2018), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), and PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020) use normalized accuracy; BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2019), and LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016) use accuracy. Recall We use the Based evaluation suite (Arora et al., 2024) and average the contains scores over SWDE (Lockard et al., 2019), FDA (Arora et al., 2023), SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2018), TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), DROP (Dua et al., 2019), and Natural Questions (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) with 2,048-token context.

sections.title: I RETRIEVAL HEAD IDENTIFICATION AND RETRIEVAL EVALUATION
sections.content: Retrieval Head identification. We apply DuoAttention-style retrieval head identification procedure (Xiao et al., 2025) to the final 510M Vanilla and BLD checkpoints. Each model has six attention layers, with two KV heads and eight query heads per layer. We learn one gate αℓ,g [0, 1] per KV head (12 gates in total), shared by its four query heads. Before the attention output projection, each head interpolates between full causal and streaming attention: (cid:101)oℓ,h = αℓ,g(h)ofull ℓ,h + (1 αℓ,g(h))ostream ℓ,h . (12) Streaming attention retains the first 128 tokens and the most recent 256 tokens, subject to causality. All pretrained parameters are frozen; KDA layers retain their original computation without gates. Each model serves as its own full-attention teacher. We optimize the gates using mean squared error between teacher and student final hidden states at reference-answer token positions, plus

Thus, masked head denotes KV head whose four query heads use restricted context, rather than head with zeroed output. The evaluated budgets are 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12 KV heads, obtained by rounding masking ratios of 0%, 10%, . . . , 100%. We use the same separately generated set of 64 documents and 10 passkeys per document for both models and every budget (640 queries per condition). Each passkey contains 32 random NATOalphabet words embedded in BookSum text. The 16K length includes the document and reference questionanswer pairs. At evaluation, each question is answered independently from the document cache using greedy decoding, without reference answers or earlier questionanswer pairs. The plotted accuracy is the percentage of queries whose first generated token matches the reference. I.1 DETAILS OF THE GRADIENT DYNAMICS EXPERIMENT Figure 5 compares never-frozen baseline with KDA-freezing intervention under the settings in Table 24. At the branching point, the frozen trajectory is split into continued-freezing and unfreezing branches with identical model, optimizer, scheduler. Unfreezing resumes the paused KDA Adam states without resetting the optimizer. Within each seed, all compared branches follow the same training-data sequence. Training uses full backward passes and the same step-specific baseline clipping coefficient before frozen updates are masked. We measure unclipped attention gradients using the same gradient-enabled diagnostic graph across conditions. For each attention mixer, we average the per-example gradient vectors before taking their ℓ2 norm, then divide by the corresponding baseline norm at the same step. The plotted statistic is the arithmetic mean of the two attention mixers trajectories, each computed as the geometric mean of paired ratios across seeds. The left panel enlarges the freezing phase of the full trajectory shown on the right.
